passage: Debates about intuition tend to fall into two camps that talk past each other. One camp collects cases in which experienced professionals, asked to explain a snap judgement, cannot say how they knew, and yet were right: the nurse who senses that a patient is deteriorating before the monitors register anything, the engineer who distrusts a design at a glance. The other camp collects cases in which confident experts did no better than simple formulas, or than chance, at predicting outcomes in their own fields. Each camp treats its own cases as the typical ones and the other camp's as curiosities.

A way through the impasse begins by asking what intuition is. On the most plausible account it is recognition: the rapid matching of a present situation to patterns stored from earlier ones, which brings with it a sense of what is likely to happen next and of what to do. Recognition of this kind can be only as good as the patterns it has learned, and patterns can be learned only where two conditions hold. The environment must contain regularities that link cues to outcomes, and the person must have had extensive practice with feedback quick and clear enough to reveal whether a judgement was right. A ward where patients either recover or worsen within hours satisfies both conditions. A market in which prices reflect the guesses of many other participants, and in which the consequences of a choice emerge slowly and mixed with luck, satisfies neither very well.

This account explains why both camps can find their cases. It also yields a less comfortable conclusion. The feeling of knowing that accompanies intuition is produced in the same way whether or not the underlying patterns are valid. A forecaster who has spent years in an environment with little regularity can feel as sure as a nurse, because confidence grows with familiarity and with the coherence of the story one can tell, not with accuracy. Subjective certainty therefore tells us almost nothing about whether to trust a judgement. What tells us something is the environment in which the judgement was learned.

The practical upshot is not that intuition should be confined to a list of approved professions. The same expert may work in a high-validity environment for some tasks and a low-validity one for others. A clinician may become very good at judging, within minutes, whether a patient needs urgent attention, while long-range predictions about the same patient's recovery, whose outcomes arrive years later and are shaped by many intervening events, remain little better than guesses. The question to ask of any intuition, then, is not who holds it or how firmly, but whether the conditions for learning it were ever present.

passage: The end of empire is usually pictured as a ceremony. A flag is lowered at midnight, another is raised, a governor boards a ship, and a new state takes its seat in the international order. Historians have long known that the picture is too tidy, and a powerful critique, voiced by some of the leaders of newly independent states themselves and given the name neo-colonialism, holds that it is not merely tidy but false. On this account, formal independence changed the personnel and the symbols of rule while leaving its substance intact: the new states still sold raw materials at prices set elsewhere, borrowed from foreign banks, bought foreign manufactures and relied on foreign advisers. The flag changed; the economy did not.

The critique captured something the ceremonial picture ignores, and it remains a useful corrective to triumphal accounts. Yet it shares more with the view it attacks than either side usually admits. Both treat empire as a single thing that either ends or persists, so that the only question is whether the moment of independence marked its end. Empire was not a single thing. It was a bundle of relations, held together by the power of the imperial state: sovereignty over territory and law, control of trade and currency, the organisation of armed force, the training of an administrative and professional class, the language in which public life was conducted, and the habits of deference and aspiration that all these produced. There is no reason to expect such strands to have come apart at the same speed, and they did not.

Sovereignty, the strand that the ceremony marked, ended at a stroke, and its ending was not trivial. A sovereign government could nationalise a foreign-owned mine, change its alliances, write a new constitution, expel a foreign base or make ruinous mistakes of its own, and many did each of these things. Other strands loosened over decades. Monetary arrangements tying several former colonies' currencies to that of the former ruler persisted long after independence; legal systems, curricula and civil-service procedures inherited from the colonial period often outlasted the governments that had installed them; the former metropolis remained, for many, the place where one went to study and to be taken seriously. Some of these continuities were imposed through unequal bargaining at the moment of transfer. Others were chosen, and defended, by new elites who had been formed by the old system and found its institutions congenial.

Seen as an unbundling, decolonisation ceases to be an event that either happened or did not, and becomes a set of processes whose timing differed by strand and by place. This has a practical as well as a historiographical consequence. The question 'When did empire end?' admits no good answer, and debates conducted in its terms tend to stall, with one side pointing to the ceremonies and the other to the trade figures. The better question is which relations were transformed, when, by whom and at what cost. It allows one to say, without contradiction, that a country became fully sovereign in a given year and that its banking system or its universities remained oriented toward its former ruler for a generation.

It also places responsibility more precisely. If the persistence of colonial patterns were simply the continuation of empire by other means, then the governments of independent states would be its passive victims. If some strands were retained by choice, those governments must answer for the choosing, just as former imperial powers must answer for the strands they kept by pressure. The unbundled view is less satisfying than either of the stories it replaces, since it yields no single date and no single villain. That is not a weakness in a historical account; it is usually a sign that the account has begun to fit its subject.

passage: Moral relativism is often defended as the natural philosophy of a tolerant person. If moral claims are true only relative to the standards of a culture, the argument runs, then no culture is in a position to condemn the practices of another, and the proper attitude towards difference is one of respectful non-interference. The appeal of this reasoning is easy to understand, since much historical cruelty was committed by people who were certain that their own customs embodied universal truth and that this certainty licensed them to remake others by force.

Yet the argument has a curious structure. Its conclusion, that we ought to tolerate other cultures, is itself a moral claim, and it is plainly meant to hold universally: the relativist does not think tolerance is required only of cultures that happen to value it. A culture whose standards prized conquest would, by relativist lights, be acting rightly when it conquered. If relativism is true, the most a tolerant culture can say to such a culture is that tolerance is valued here, which is a report about itself rather than a reason addressed to anyone else. The relativist who wants tolerance to bind everyone has quietly helped himself to a non-relative principle.

None of this shows that relativism is false, and the defender has a reply. Perhaps the claim is not that relativism entails tolerance but that believing it tends to produce tolerant people, by weakening the confidence that fuels crusades. That may be true as a matter of psychology, though the historical record is mixed; doubt can make people gentle, but it can also leave them unable to object to anything at all. More importantly, the reply changes the subject. It defends relativism as a useful belief rather than a true one, and it concedes that the case for tolerance must be made on other grounds.

Those other grounds are not hard to find. One can hold that some moral claims are true for everyone and still think that humility about one's own judgements, respect for people's capacity to govern their own lives, and the dismal record of forced conversion all count strongly against intervention in most cases. Such a view is less comfortable than relativism, because it obliges one to say that some practices are wrong even while declining to stamp them out. But it has the advantage of being able to explain why tolerance matters, which relativism, for all its tolerant intentions, cannot.

options.C: justify intervening by force to protect the peoples that the conquering culture threatens.

passage: Imagine a cinema that sells popcorn in two sizes: a small tub at a modest price and a large tub at nearly twice that. Most customers buy the small one, until the cinema adds a third option, a medium tub priced only slightly below the large. Hardly anyone buys the medium, yet sales of the large tub rise sharply, so that the new option has done its work without ever being chosen. It exists to make the large tub look like a bargain, and in many such cases it succeeds; marketers call such an option a decoy, and the pattern it produces turns up often enough, with magazine subscriptions, holiday packages and software plans as well as snacks, to deserve a more careful explanation than the claim that customers are easily fooled.

The standard account of choice in economics assumes that a person arrives at a shop with a ranking of the available goods already settled, and that the shop merely reveals it. On that account the decoy should be inert: if I prefer the small tub to the large one, the arrival of a medium tub that I do not want should leave my ranking of the other two untouched. What the decoy suggests instead is that many preferences are not retrieved but assembled on the spot, from the comparisons the menu makes easy. The medium tub is easy to compare with the large, being the same product at almost the same price with visibly less popcorn, whereas the comparison between the small and the large, which requires trading money against quantity, is considerably harder. Consequently, people lean on the easy comparison and let it settle the hard one.

It would be a mistake to conclude that preferences are endlessly pliable, for the effect is strongest when buyers are unsure what they want and have little experience of the product; a regular who knows exactly how much popcorn she can eat is rarely moved. It also weakens when the decoy is so plainly inferior that customers notice the trick, and resentment at being steered can push them the other way. These limits matter, because they show that the decoy exploits a gap in knowledge rather than a defect of reason: constructing a preference out of whatever comparisons are available is a perfectly sensible strategy for someone who lacks better information.

The more interesting lesson concerns the menu itself. We usually treat the set of options as neutral background and the decision as the thing to be explained, but the decoy shows that the background is part of the decision. Whoever arranges the options, whether a cinema, a software firm setting its subscription tiers or a restaurant pricing its wine list, is not merely displaying choices but helping to form them. This does not make every arrangement sinister, since some arrangement is unavoidable, but it does mean that the question of what people chose cannot be separated from the question of what they were shown.

passage: Why does a string quartet cost so much more to hear today, relative to a shirt or a radio, than it did a century ago? Not because the musicians have become greedy or the concert halls inefficient. Performing a quartet required four players and roughly forty minutes then, and it requires the same now; no innovation has allowed three musicians to play it in half the time without destroying the thing being bought. Meanwhile workers in manufacturing have become many times more productive, and their wages have risen accordingly. The musicians' pay must rise too, or they would drift into other work. So the price of the quartet climbs relative to goods whose production has been transformed, even though nothing about the quartet has changed.

Economists sometimes call this the cost disease, and its reach goes far beyond concert halls. Teaching, nursing, care of the elderly and much legal and administrative work share the quartet's structure: the service largely consists of a person's time and attention, and attempts to compress that time often degrade what is delivered. A class of sixty is cheaper per pupil than a class of thirty, but it is not the same product at a lower price. Where productivity in such sectors lags, their share of national spending rises, and with it a persistent suspicion that schools and hospitals are squandering money, since nearly everything else seems to be getting cheaper.

The diagnosis contains a consolation that is often missed. If the relative cost of services rises because the rest of the economy has become more productive, then society as a whole is richer, and can afford those services even at their higher relative price. A family that spends a larger share of its income on its children's schooling than its grandparents did may also own far more and work fewer hours. What feels like a crisis of affordability is, on this view, partly a change in the composition of a growing budget.

The argument should not be stretched into a blanket excuse. That some cost growth in services is unavoidable does not mean that all of it is; administrative layers can multiply in a hospital as easily as in any other organisation, and the cost disease offers them no defence. Nor is the consolation automatic. The higher relative price of care falls hardest on those whose incomes have not shared in the general gain, and public budgets that depend on taxes voters resist may cut services long before the arithmetic says they must. The cost disease explains a pattern; it does not settle who should pay for it.

passage: The names we give to periods of the past look like neutral conveniences, markers on a timeline that allow us to say roughly when something happened. In fact most of them are compressed arguments. 'The Middle Ages' is the clearest case. The phrase took hold among European writers who believed that they were reviving the learning of the ancient world after a long interruption, and who therefore saw the intervening thousand years as an interval, a middle that mattered chiefly as the gap between two moments of achievement. A period named in this way has been judged before it has been studied.

Generations of historians have since shown how little that judgement fits the evidence. The centuries in question saw the founding of universities, the building of great cathedrals, the elaboration of law and the slow growth of towns and trade; far from being an interruption, they laid much of the ground on which later achievements stood. Yet the name has survived the demolition of the view that produced it, and it continues to whisper that the period was something to be got through. Words outlast the arguments that coined them.

The difficulty grows when such a label is exported. To speak of a 'medieval' period in the history of a region far from Europe is to import a chronology built for one part of the world, with its own sense of what came before and after, and to invite the historian to look there for whatever the label suggests, such as a decline and a later rebirth, whether or not the evidence of that region points to anything of the kind.

It does not follow that we should try to do without period names. History cannot be written without some way of grouping years together, and the alternatives are not innocent either: centuries are as arbitrary as any label, cutting through lives and movements at points chosen by arithmetic, and they bring a peculiar habit of their own, the tendency to treat each hundred years as having a single character. The sensible course is to keep the names while holding them lightly, treating each as a hypothesis about what a stretch of time had in common, to be tested against the evidence and abandoned where it fails. The danger lies not in having labels but in letting the label arrive before the research and decide what the research will look for.

passage: Arguments about public statues tend to be conducted as if there were only two positions. On one side are those who say that the statue of a figure now held in disrepute should come down, because a city ought not to go on honouring what it has come to find shameful. On the other are those who say that removing it 'erases history', and that a mature society learns from its past instead of hiding it. The quarrel is loud, and it is often bitter, because each side suspects the other of bad faith: of wishing to rewrite the past, or of wishing to keep its injustices on a pedestal. Each side assumes it knows what a statue is. Neither, I think, quite does.

A statue is not a history lesson. It records almost nothing about the life of its subject: a name, a pair of dates, perhaps a line of praise. What it records very precisely is a decision, taken at a particular moment by particular people, to honour that subject in that place. Many of the statues now in dispute were raised long after the events they commemorate, often by committees with purposes of their own, such as asserting the standing of a group or a cause at a time when that standing was being questioned. A statue is therefore better evidence about the people who raised it than about the person it depicts.

Seen in this light, the charge of erasing history loses much of its force. Taking a statue down does not alter what happened, and the books, records and family memories that tell its subject's story remain where they were. What removal changes is a present act of honour, and every generation is entitled to reconsider whom it honours. Yet the other camp should not feel wholly vindicated. A statue that is quietly carted away also removes evidence of what an earlier generation chose to celebrate, and that evidence can be uncomfortable in useful ways, reminding a city that the values it now rejects were once publicly and confidently held by respectable people.

The popular compromise of leaving the statue in place and adding an explanatory plaque is often presented as the neutral option. It is not. A plaque is also an editorial act: someone must decide what it says, how long it is and whose judgement it expresses, and a few lines of small print beneath a towering bronze figure rarely win the argument with it. Moving a statue to a museum, where the date and purpose of its making can be displayed alongside it, may come closer to keeping the evidence without continuing the honour. Whatever a community decides, it should at least be clear that it is deciding how to honour, not whether to remember.

options.B: the main achievements of its subject, set down in a form that passers-by can easily read.
options.C: the settled judgement of an entire community about the moral worth of the person it depicts.
options.D: a choice, made by certain people at a certain time, to honour its subject in that place.

passage: For much of the twentieth century, forest agencies in several countries treated fire as an enemy to be defeated wherever it appeared. The logic seemed unanswerable: fire destroys timber, threatens homes and kills animals, so every fire extinguished was a loss averted. Agencies measured their performance by how quickly they put fires out and how few hectares burned, and by those measures many of them succeeded remarkably well. Lookout towers, firebreaks and crews ready to move at short notice made it possible to reach most fires while they were still small.

The success contained its own reversal. In many dry forests, frequent fires of low intensity had once cleared the undergrowth, fallen branches and young trees that gather on the forest floor, while leaving the older, thick-barked trees largely unharmed. When such fires were suppressed year after year, that material was left to build up. The forest grew denser, and the fuel that would once have burned off in small, manageable fires accumulated until, in a hot, dry season, a fire that could not be stopped found enough of it to climb into the crowns of the trees. Such fires kill the very trees that the earlier, smaller ones had spared. By preventing many small fires, suppression had, in effect, been saving up for a few enormous ones.

The lesson is sometimes drawn too broadly. Not every ecosystem evolved with frequent fire; in some wet forests and many shrublands fire was historically rare, and a recent increase in burning there is a threat rather than a return to normal. Nor does the history of suppression explain every catastrophic fire, since drought, heat and the spread of housing into wooded land matter as well. The argument is not that fire is good, but that whether a given fire is harmful depends on the ecosystem in which it burns and on that ecosystem's history.

Recognising this has not made the remedy easy. Deliberately setting fires under controlled conditions, or allowing some natural fires to burn, can reduce accumulated fuel, but it carries risks that suppression appeared not to. Politically, a season without burning looks like competence. Smoke drifts over towns, and a planned burn that escapes is blamed on the people who lit it, while a wildfire that grows from decades of accumulated fuel is blamed on nature. A manager therefore faces an asymmetry. The harm of acting is visible and attributable; the harm of not acting is deferred and diffuse, and the easiest course is to keep doing what made the problem worse.

passage: That most citizens know little about the policies they vote on is one of the most frequently confirmed observations about modern democracies, and one of the least surprising. A single vote almost never decides an election, and the hours needed to master the details of tax law or trade policy are hours taken from work, family and sleep. Ignorance, in these circumstances, is not a failure of character. It is what a sensible person would choose if he or she treated the vote as a decision with private costs and a vanishingly small chance of making a difference. Economists call this rational ignorance, and the label is apt: the problem is not that voters reason badly but that they have little reason to acquire what good reasoning would need.

Two very different conclusions are drawn from this. The first, which has gained a certain academic following, is that the franchise should be weighted towards those who know more, since a decision made by the informed is likely to be better than one made by everyone. The second, more common among defenders of democracy, is that ignorance matters less than it seems, because voters rely on shortcuts. They need not study a programme if they know which party proposed it; they need not understand monetary policy to notice whether prices are rising; they can follow the advice of an organisation they trust. A voter equipped with such cues, the argument goes, can vote much as she would if she were fully informed.

The second conclusion is more attractive than the first, but it claims too much. A shortcut is only as good as the connection between the cue and the thing the voter actually cares about, and that connection is not guaranteed. Party labels are informative when parties are stable and their programmes distinct; when parties fragment or converge, the label says little. Judging a government by how things are going is reasonable if the government controls how things are going, but voters who punish an incumbent for a drought, or for a downturn that began abroad, are using a cue that measures luck as much as competence. And an endorsement is valuable only if the endorser shares the voter's interests, which is precisely what a well-funded campaign may try to disguise. Shortcuts, in short, do not make ignorance harmless; they make its effects depend on the environment in which voters find themselves.

That dependence, however, is also the strongest reply to those who would ration the vote. If the quality of popular judgement varies with the reliability of the cues available, then the natural remedy is to improve the cues rather than to disqualify the people who use them. Parties with clear and lasting identities, intermediaries whose interests are visible, a press that reports what governments actually control: each of these makes ordinary shortcuts more trustworthy. Weighting votes by knowledge, by contrast, would leave the environment of cues untouched while inviting a quarrel, unlikely ever to be settled impartially, about who should set the test and what it should contain.

Neither side, then, has quite grasped the problem. The critics are right that an uninformed electorate can be misled, and the defenders are right that citizens need not be experts to judge well. What both overlook is that the competence of voters is not a fixed property of individuals but partly a product of institutions, and that a democracy can therefore make its citizens wiser as voters without making any of them more learned.

passage: Translators of the great books of the past often remark on a puzzle. The original of an old epic or a classical tragedy does not seem to age; readers return to it century after century and find it as alive as ever. Yet translations of the same work date quickly. A version that seemed fresh to its first readers can sound stiff or quaint within a lifetime, and every generation or two a new one appears, prefaced by the claim that its predecessors have become unreadable. Why should the copy age when the original, which is older and in many ways stranger, does not? The question is worth more attention than it usually receives, because the answer says something about what a translation is.

The usual answer is linguistic: a translation is written in the language of its own moment, with that moment's idioms and its notions of what sounds dignified and what sounds plain, and these change. The original, by contrast, has been absorbed into a tradition that reads it as a historical text and forgives its strangeness. There is truth in this, but it cannot be the whole story, since old translations are often perfectly intelligible and still feel inadequate.

A deeper reason lies in what translation requires. A great work is full of places where its sense is undecided: a word that could mean anger or grief, a line whose tone could be mocking or tender, a scene whose moral weight is left to the reader. The original can leave such places open, and much of its power to sustain rereading comes from that openness; a translator has no such freedom, because writing in another language forces choices at every point, and each choice settles a question the original left unsettled. The choices are not arbitrary, but they are shaped by what the translator's own age finds plausible or important, and so the translation records one generation's reading of the work. When the concerns of that generation fade, its translation comes to look like what it always was: an interpretation.

Seen in this light, retranslation is not a sign that earlier translators failed. It is one of the ways a classic stays alive, each version making a fresh set of decisions and so showing a new reader something the others concealed. There is even an occasional reversal. Some translations become works of literature in their own right, read not as windows onto the original but for their own sake, and these, curiously, stop ageing in the way translations usually do; they come to be read, like originals, as historical texts. Their choices no longer look like a period's mistakes about another book; they look like the permanent features of a book of their own.

passage: We tend to picture hospitality as the purest form of generosity: a door opened to someone who has no claim on us and nothing to give in return. The picture is not false, but it omits half of what the practice involves. In the many traditions in which welcoming strangers is held to be a sacred duty, the welcome is also a careful exercise of authority. The host decides where the guest will sit, what he will eat, when he will speak and, eventually, when he will leave. To accept hospitality is to accept, for a time, a place inside someone else's order.

This asymmetry is not incidental. A stranger arriving at a settlement is, from the settlement's point of view, an unknown quantity: he may be a trader, a refugee, a spy or a raider. Hospitality converts this uncertain figure into a guest, someone whose position is defined and whose conduct is now governed by rules that the host administers. The rituals that so often accompany a welcome, such as the offering of water, the sharing of salt or bread and the formal exchange of names, can be read as stages in this conversion. The guest who eats at the host's table has implicitly agreed not to harm the household, and the host, in turn, has made himself responsible for the guest's safety against third parties.

It is significant, too, that hospitality is so often limited in time. Many customs specify that a guest may stay a few days before his status must change; after that he becomes a dependant who works, a kinsman by adoption, or simply an unwelcome burden. The welcome is generous precisely because it is temporary. A guest who could stay forever on a guest's terms would gradually unsettle the household's order, and the host would cease to be master of his own house.

Some philosophers have pressed for an ideal of unconditional hospitality, a welcome that asks no questions and sets no limits. As a corrective to the suspicion with which outsiders are often treated, the ideal has force. But taken literally it would dissolve the very relation it seeks to purify. Hospitality requires a host, someone who is at home and who can therefore offer a place; if every condition is removed, there is no longer anyone in a position to welcome. The authority that makes us uneasy is not a corruption of hospitality. It is the condition that allows a stranger to be received at all.

passage: A familiar complaint holds that the theory of natural selection is empty at its core. Its slogan, survival of the fittest, seems to define the fittest as those who survive, so that the principle reduces to the statement that survivors survive. A claim that cannot be false, the complaint continues, explains nothing; it merely relabels what happened. The objection is old, and it has a certain surface appeal, but it depends on running together two different things: the record of which organisms in fact left offspring and the properties that made them likely to do so.

Consider two moths of the same species, one pale and one dark, resting on bark darkened by soot. The dark moth is fitter in that setting, but not because it happens to have left more offspring. It is fitter because its colouring makes it harder for birds to see, and that is a fact one can establish independently, by measuring how often birds find each kind of moth on each kind of bark. Fitness, properly understood, is a propensity: an expected rate of reproduction given an organism's traits and its surroundings. Like the fragility of a glass, it is a disposition that holds whether or not it is ever displayed. A fragile glass may survive a lifetime on a shelf, and a well-camouflaged moth may die in an unlucky accident; neither fact refutes the disposition.

Seen this way, the theory makes claims that could turn out false. It predicts that when the propensities of variants differ, and the differences are heritable, the frequencies of the variants will shift in a direction one can anticipate from an engineering or ecological analysis of the traits. Such predictions are tested constantly, and some fail, which is precisely what a tautology could never do. The distinction also explains why biologists speak of drift: in small populations the lucky can outbreed the fit, and the actual record of reproduction can depart from the expected one. If fitness simply meant survival, drift would be unintelligible, since there would be no gap between expectation and outcome for chance to fill.

The critics are not wholly wrong, however. Biologists often measure fitness by counting offspring, because propensities are hard to observe directly, and careless writing can slide from the measurement to the definition. The remedy is not to abandon the concept but to keep the evidence for a disposition distinct from the disposition itself.

passage: For much of the last century, efforts to explain science to the public rested on a simple picture. People who resisted a scientific conclusion, it was assumed, did so because they did not understand it; the gap between expert and lay opinion was a gap in knowledge, and it could be closed by supplying the missing facts. Critics later gave this picture a name, the deficit model, and the name stuck because it captured what was wrong with it: it treated the public as a vessel with a hole in it, defined entirely by what it lacked.

The model fails first on its own terms. If resistance came from ignorance, those who knew most about a contested subject would be the most accepting of the expert view, yet it is easy to find people who have read widely on a topic and still reject the consensus, sometimes with more conviction than before they began. Knowledge, it turns out, can be recruited to defend a position as readily as to change it. A person who already distrusts the source of a claim does not experience new information as enlightenment; she experiences it as further pressure from that source. The facts are heard, but they are heard as moves in a contest whose sides were chosen before the conversation began.

The deeper failure concerns what the model leaves out. Consider a village told by a team of engineers that a new dam upstream poses no danger. The villagers may follow the hydrology perfectly well. What they also know, and what the engineers' presentation omits, is that the last assurance they received from officials turned out to be wrong, that the benefits of the dam will flow to a distant city, and that if anything goes wrong it is they, not the engineers, who will bear the loss. Their scepticism is not a vacancy waiting to be filled. It is a judgement about whom to trust and who pays, and it may be quite rational even when the hydrology is sound.

None of this means that facts are irrelevant or that every misunderstanding is secretly a stance about power. Some people do hold mistaken beliefs simply because nobody has explained a matter clearly, and for them a good explanation is exactly what is needed. The error of the deficit model was to make this the whole story. Communication that begins by asking what an audience already knows, fears and has experienced will sometimes end in explanation. But it will at least explain the right thing, and it will treat the people it addresses as parties to a decision rather than as containers for information.

passage: Few questions in criticism have been argued so long, or with so little sign of settlement, as whether the meaning of a work is what its author intended. The intentionalist says yes: a text is an utterance, utterances are made by someone for a purpose, and to ignore that purpose is to read not the work but a sequence of marks that happens to resemble it. The anti-intentionalist says no: the author's state of mind is usually unavailable, frequently confused and in any case beside the point, since a published work belongs to the public language in which it was written, and its meaning is whatever that language, competently read, makes of it.

Each side wins its arguments by making the other's view look absurd, and each is right about what it denies. The intentionalist is right that we cannot read without attributing purposes. To notice that a sentence is ironic, that a repetition is deliberate or that a sudden plainness of style marks a turning point is already to treat the text as the product of choices; strip away every assumption about purpose and the irony vanishes along with the design. The anti-intentionalist is right that a letter to a newspaper or a diary entry in which the author explains what the book means has no special authority over the book. Authors misremember, revise their motives after the fact and sometimes simply misjudge what they have made.

The mistake common to both is to picture intention as a private event lying behind the text, which the text either reports faithfully or conceals. Intention in writing is better understood the way we understand it in action. We do not usually discover what someone meant by watching them and then consulting their inner life; we read the purpose in the shape of what they did. In the same way the intentions that matter to criticism are those embodied in a work's choices, its emphases and omissions, the expectations it sets up and then disappoints. They are public because the work is.

This view does not make the author irrelevant, nor does it make the author final. A writer's notebooks may help us see a pattern we had missed, as the testimony of a witness may help a court, but the evidence is then the pattern, not the testimony. And a work may carry implications its author never foresaw and would perhaps have disowned: a novel written to celebrate a way of life can, through the very details it lovingly records, reveal the costs that way of life imposed on those at its margins. To point this out is not to defy the author's intention but to take the work's design more seriously than its author's later account of it.

passage: It is tempting to treat superstition as a residue of ignorance, a set of mistaken beliefs that education will eventually wash away. The difficulty with this view is that superstition does not distribute itself the way ignorance does. Highly trained surgeons, pilots, stage actors and professional athletes, people who know a great deal about the causal workings of their craft, are often among the most attached to private rituals: a particular pair of socks, a fixed sequence of gestures before a performance, a refusal to say certain words aloud. If superstition were merely a gap in knowledge, these would be the last people we would expect to keep it.

A more useful observation is that superstition gathers where two conditions meet: the outcome matters a great deal, and a significant part of it lies beyond the actor's control. Ethnographers have described fishing communities that use no protective magic when they work in a sheltered lagoon, where skill reliably brings a catch, yet surround voyages into the open sea with elaborate rites. The same people hold the same beliefs about the world; what changes is their exposure to chance. Examinations, sporting finals and opening nights share this structure. Preparation counts, but on the day itself something unaccountable remains, and the ritual fills the space that preparation cannot reach.

What the ritual supplies, on this account, is not a causal lever over the outcome but a way of acting when no further useful action is available. Anxiety in the face of uncertainty tends to seek an outlet, and an outlet that is fixed, brief and familiar is better than one that is improvised, such as a last-minute change to a plan that was sound. A tennis player who bounces the ball exactly the same number of times before every serve is not, in any serious sense, trying to bend the laws of physics. She is marking a boundary between deliberation and execution, and the routine protects the execution from second thoughts.

None of this makes superstition harmless. The same disposition that steadies a performer can lead a patient to choose a charm over a treatment that works, or a trader to mistake a lucky streak for a method. The line falls roughly where the ritual stops occupying the residue of chance and begins to displace action that would genuinely improve the odds. Understood this way, superstition is neither a quaint error to be laughed at nor a hidden wisdom to be celebrated, but a predictable human response to exposure that deserves to be judged by what it crowds out.

passage: Conservation laws are usually taught as the bedrock of physics. Energy is neither created nor destroyed; momentum lost by one body is gained by another; a spinning skater who draws in her arms turns faster because her angular momentum cannot change. Presented in this way, the laws look like the deepest facts we possess, discovered by patient measurement and accepted because nature has never been caught breaking them. A theorem proved in 1918 by the mathematician Emmy Noether suggests that this presentation, though not wrong, puts the foundations in the wrong place.

What Noether showed is that, for any system whose laws can be written in a certain standard mathematical form, every continuous symmetry of those laws corresponds to a quantity that is conserved. If the laws are the same today as they were yesterday, energy is conserved. If they are the same here as in the next room, momentum is conserved. If they do not depend on which way a system happens to be facing, angular momentum is conserved. The conservation laws, in other words, are not separate facts standing side by side; they are consequences of a single kind of fact, namely that the rules of nature do not care when, where or in what orientation they are applied.

It is tempting to conclude that conservation has thereby been proved, that energy must be conserved as a matter of logic. That would be a mistake. The theorem converts one question into another; it does not settle either. Whether the laws really are the same at all times is something only observation can tell us, and the theorem ensures that the evidence for the symmetry and the evidence for the conservation law are, in effect, the same evidence. What has changed is the direction of explanation. We no longer say that energy is conserved and leave the matter there; we say that energy is conserved because time is uniform, and we are then free to ask whether time is uniform.

That question has teeth. On the scale of the whole universe, which is expanding and so does not look the same from one epoch to the next, the symmetry behind energy conservation is not obviously present, and it is far from clear that a universal law of energy conservation can even be stated there. On the older view this would look like a scandal, a crack in the bedrock. On the view the theorem encourages, it is just what one should expect: where the symmetry fails, the conservation law loses its footing, and the surprise would be if it did not. A principle that once seemed beyond question has become something more useful, a claim whose limits can be foreseen.

passage: Few findings in social psychology have escaped the laboratory as completely as the bystander effect. In its popular form it says that the more people witness an emergency, the less likely the victim is to receive help, and it is usually offered as evidence of modern apathy: crowds of onlookers, each waiting for someone else to act. The idea owes much of its fame to a newspaper account of a murder in a city street in the 1960s, in which dozens of neighbours were said to have watched and done nothing. Later investigation suggested that the account greatly exaggerated both the number of witnesses and their indifference, but by then the story had become a parable.

The experiments that followed were more careful than the parable. Their central claim was not that people are callous but that responsibility, when shared, is diluted. A person who believes that she alone has heard a cry for help knows that if she does not act, no one will; a person who knows that others have heard it can reasonably suppose that someone better placed is already responding. Ambiguity compounds the effect. In a group, each witness looks to the others to work out whether anything is really wrong, and the calm faces of people who are themselves only watching can persuade everyone that nothing is.

Yet there is a gap between what these studies measured and what the popular version claims. They showed that a given individual is less likely to help when others are present. They did not show that a victim is less likely to be helped. The two come apart because a crowd contains many potential helpers: even if each one is somewhat less willing, the chance that at least one of them steps forward can remain high, and may rise as the crowd grows. Some recent studies of recorded conflicts in public places have reported that in most of them at least one bystander intervened, a pattern hard to reconcile with the image of the paralysed crowd.

None of this makes the original research worthless. The mechanisms it identified are real, and they help explain why emergencies in which no one is sure what is happening, or whose job it is to act, can go unanswered. What it does not support is a sweeping verdict on human nature. The practical advice that follows from the research is modest and useful: if you need help, single out one person and tell that person what to do, so that responsibility is no longer shared and the situation is no longer ambiguous.

passage: Defenders of live theatre, when pressed to explain why anyone should purchase an expensive ticket to see what could be watched more cheaply and comfortably on a screen, usually appeal to presence. The actors are there, in the same room, breathing the same air; on screen they are only images. The answer is sincere, but considered as an argument it is considerably weaker than it sounds. A great many things are physically present to us without being valuable for that reason, and a lecture delivered in person is not obviously better than the same lecture recorded. If presence were all that distinguished the stage, the case for theatre would rest on something close to a superstition about physical proximity.

A more promising answer begins from what presence makes possible. A filmed performance is complete before any viewer encounters it; nothing the viewer does, however attentive or distracted, can reach back and alter it. A stage performance is still being made while the audience watches, and the audience is among the conditions under which it is made. Actors in a comedy learn to hold a line until the laughter at the previous one has crested and begun to fall, and the length of that pause differs from night to night because the laughter does. In a tense scene, a silence of a particular quality in the house tells the performers that they have the room, and they may let a moment stretch further than they would before a restless audience. These adjustments are individually small, but cumulatively they mean that a stage performance can be, in part, a response to the particular people assembled to witness it.

The audience, moreover, is conscious of this reciprocity. Spectators in a theatre are aware that they can be heard and, in an intimate space, seen; they are also aware of one another, and a laugh that spreads along a row, or fails to, shapes what each person feels. The experience is less that of watching an object than of taking part, in a minor and mostly silent way, in an event whose outcome is not wholly settled. That is why a performance can fail in the theatre in a way that a film cannot: not through a flaw in its making, which a film may also have, but through a breakdown between stage and house.

It may be objected that this account flatters most actual theatre, which is rarely so delicately attuned to its spectators. Many productions are drilled to such precision that they vary little from night to night, and in a large commercial house the performers can barely see past the first rows. That is true, and it calls for a qualification rather than a retraction. The responsiveness described here is a capacity of the live form, not a guarantee; a production can choose to use it or to suppress it, and one that suppresses it entirely has given up the main thing that the stage offers and the screen does not. Film, meanwhile, has resources of its own, the close-up and the edit among them, and nothing here implies that it is a lesser art.

The case for live theatre, then, is not that the actors are physically near but that the performance and its audience remain capable of affecting one another. It follows, perhaps uncomfortably for some institutions, that the strongest argument for theatre is simultaneously a demand upon it. A theatre that wishes to justify its prices by appealing to liveness owes its audience a performance in which liveness actually does some work.

passage: The argument for protecting infant industries is older than most of the arguments now made against it, and it is more respectable than its critics often allow. Its premise is that productivity in many industries is learned rather than given. A new steelworks or shipyard in a country without one begins with inexperienced workers, untested managers and suppliers who do not yet know what it needs; it will make costly mistakes for years before it reaches the efficiency of established foreign rivals. If it must meet those rivals at once, it may never survive long enough to learn. A period of protection, on this view, is not a subsidy to inefficiency but an investment in the learning that will eventually remove it.

The argument gains force from a further point. Much of what a pioneering firm learns does not stay inside it. Workers it trains move to competitors, suppliers it develops go on to serve other customers, and the mere demonstration that an industry can work in a given place lowers the risk for those who follow. Over time a cluster of related firms may form around the pioneer, each drawing on skills that the pioneer paid to create. Because the pioneer bears the cost of this learning but captures only part of its benefit, an unaided market will produce too little of it, and there is a case in principle for public support.

The difficulty lies not in the logic but in the ending. Protection is granted on the promise that it is temporary, yet every year it lasts it builds a constituency for its continuation: owners whose profits depend on it, workers whose jobs appear to, and officials whose standing is tied to the industry's survival. Worse, the protection itself weakens the motive to learn. A firm that knows its shelter will be extended whenever it fails to become competitive has little reason to bear the pain of becoming so, and the infant can remain an infant indefinitely, growing larger without growing up. The many cases in which protection outlived any plausible learning period are not accidents of bad administration; they are what the incentives predict.

It follows that the argument stands or falls on whether the exit can be made credible in advance. Protection whose duration is fixed and public, whose renewal depends on measurable progress, and whose beneficiaries are required to compete in some market where the shelter does not reach them, such as export markets, is a different policy from protection granted open-endedly. Export performance is especially revealing, because a firm cannot fake competitiveness in a market it does not control. A protected firm that must also sell abroad, at prices set by rivals it cannot shut out, learns quickly whether it has improved, and so does the government that shelters it. The interesting historical question is therefore not whether successful industrialisers protected their industries, since many did, but whether they attached conditions that forced the protected firms to improve.

None of this makes the conditions easy to impose. Withdrawing support from a large employer that has missed its targets requires a government able to bear the political cost, and the very constituency that protection creates is what makes that cost high. Protection also has victims who are easy to overlook: the firms that must buy the sheltered product at a higher price, and whose own competitiveness suffers as a result. The infant-industry case, then, is best understood not as a general licence but as a demanding bargain, sound in theory and available in practice only to states that can enforce its terms.

passage: Few facts about music are more familiar, or more puzzling on reflection, than the willingness of listeners to seek out music that makes them sad. People do not, on the whole, go looking for grief or disappointment in the rest of life, and they would think it odd to be offered a sorrowful afternoon as a treat. Yet slow laments, songs of loss and the darker movements of symphonies are among the most loved music in many traditions, and listeners return to them deliberately.

One response dissolves the puzzle by denying its premise. On this view the listener does not really feel sad at all; she recognises sadness in the music, much as she might recognise a sorrowful expression on a carved mask, and what she enjoys is the beauty and skill with which the sadness is expressed. The view has the merit of explaining why sad music does not ruin anyone's day. But it fits poorly with what many listeners report, which is that they are moved, sometimes to tears, and not merely informed. A second response accepts that the feeling is real and explains the pleasure by the frame around it: the sadness arrives without a loss to cause it and without consequences to follow, so it can be savoured in a way that the sadness of life cannot.

Both responses capture something, but both treat the emotion as a single state, present or absent, mild or intense. What music does with an emotion is closer to giving it a shape over time. A lament does not simply announce sorrow; it gathers, rises, breaks, returns to a phrase heard earlier and comes to rest. The listener who follows it is led through a version of sorrow that has a beginning, an end and a recognisable order, which is precisely what the sorrows of ordinary life usually lack. The pleasure, on this account, lies less in the feeling than in the form the feeling is given.

This does not mean that sad music always pleases, or pleases everyone. Many people who are grieving find that they cannot listen to the music they loved before, at least for a time, and their experience is a useful check on any theory. A frame that keeps sadness at a safe distance should make such music easier to bear in grief, not harder. The account offered here does better: a shaped and completed sorrow may be unbearable to someone whose own sorrow has no shape yet, because the contrast is too sharp.
